chapters.title: Chapter 6: After Filing: Refunds, Notices and Fixing Mistakes

lessons.title: Tracking Your Refund and Reading the Section 143(1) Intimation

body.text: Your return is a claim, not a verdict. The department decides what it accepts when it processes the return, and tells you in one email. Most people never open it.

markDefs.definition: The automated communication sent after your return is processed, comparing the figures you reported with the figures the department computed, and showing a refund, a demand, or neither.

children.text: Once you e-verify, your return goes to the Centralized Processing Centre in Bengaluru. Its systems check your arithmetic, match your tax credits against Form 26AS and look for claims that do not add up. The result arrives as an
of the Income-tax Act, 1961, which still governs FY 2025-26 returns. From Tax Year 2026-27, the same processing sits in Section 270 of the Income-tax Act, 2025.

events.title: Return e-Verified
events.description: The status changes to successfully e-verified. Nothing else is needed from you for now.

events.title: Return Processed
events.description: CPC processes the return. Refunds are commonly credited around four to five weeks after verification, though it can take longer.

events.title: Intimation Emailed
events.description: The intimation reaches your registered email, with a copy available on the portal. Open it the day it arrives.

events.title: Refund Credited or Demand Raised
events.description: A refund goes to your pre-validated bank account. A demand must be paid or disputed.

events.title: Nine Months
events.description: The intimation must be issued within nine months from the end of the financial year in which you filed. For a return filed in July 2026, that is 31 December 2027.

stats.label: Outer Limit to Process
stats.context: From the end of the financial year of filing

stats.label: Intimation Password
stats.context: PAN in lower case, then DDMMYYYY

children.text: The intimation is a two-column table. One column is what you reported. The other is what the department computed. Read across each row and stop at the first row where the two numbers differ. That difference is the entire story of the intimation.

body.caption: An Intimation for AY 2026-27: Ramesh, a Salaried Filer in Kanpur

cells: Income from salary
Income from other sources
Total income
Total tax and cess
TDS credit claimed
Refund

body.title: Why Is the Refund Smaller?
body.prompt: Ramesh claimed TDS of ₹48,000, but his Form 26AS shows only ₹44,500, because one deductor had not filed its TDS return when the department processed his ITR. By how much has his refund been reduced?
body.explanation: ₹48,000 less ₹44,500 is ₹3,500. His income and tax were accepted in full, and only the tax credit was cut, so his refund falls from ₹12,000 to ₹8,500. Once the deductor files its correction and the credit appears in Form 26AS, Ramesh can file a rectification request to claim the remaining ₹3,500.

body.caption: Why Intimations Most Often Differ From the Return

cells: TDS credit reduced
Tax credit lower than claimed
Check Form 26AS, then chase the deductor to file or correct its TDS return and seek rectification
Income added
Interest or other income you left out is included
Compare with AIS. If the addition is right, pay the demand
Deduction disallowed
A deduction claimed is reduced or removed
Check that it is allowed in your regime and that the details entered were complete
Arithmetic corrected
Totals differ from yours
Usually a genuine slip in a manually edited figure
Interest or late fee added
Interest for advance tax default, or a late fee
Recompute using Chapter 5, and pay if it is correct
Refund adjusted against old demand
Refund reduced by a demand from an earlier year
You should receive a separate intimation first, so respond before the adjustment is made

body.text: An intimation showing no refund and no demand is good news, not a notice. It means the department agrees with your return. Save the PDF: it is the cleanest proof that your return was accepted as filed.

children.text: When You Disagree With the Intimation

columns.label: Rectification Request
points: For a mistake apparent from the record, such as a TDS credit that exists in Form 26AS but was not given
Filed on the portal under Services, then Rectification, against the intimation
Section 154 of the 1961 Act, which becomes Section 287 of the Income-tax Act, 2025
Does not let you change what you originally reported

columns.label: Revised Return
points: For your own error or omission, such as income you forgot to report
Filed as a fresh return under the revised return provisions
Replaces the return itself, and is processed again from scratch
Subject to its own deadline, covered in the next lesson

body.title: Pick the Right Remedy
body.question: Anita found that her intimation disallowed a ₹25,000 deduction for health insurance. Checking her return, she sees she entered the premium but left the insurer policy number blank. What should she do?
options: File a rectification request, since the deduction is genuine
File a revised return with complete details, because the omission was in her own return
Ignore it, as intimations are only informational
body.explanation: Rectification is for mistakes apparent from the record, not for supplying information she never gave. Because the gap is in her own return, a revised return with complete details is the right route, provided the deadline for revising has not passed. An appeal is a much later step, and ignoring an intimation that raises a demand only adds interest.

body.text: If the intimation raises a demand, respond within the time the notice specifies rather than letting it sit. On the portal, go to Pending Actions, then Response to Outstanding Demand, and either agree and pay, or disagree with reasons. An unanswered demand grows with interest and can be set off against future refunds under Section 245 of the 1961 Act, re-enacted as Section 438 of the Income-tax Act, 2025.

body.caption: Why Refunds Fail, and the Fix

cells: Bank account not pre-validated, or validated but never nominated for refund
Validate it under My Bank Account and tick it for refund
Account closed, or IFSC changed after a bank merger
Add a current account and raise a refund reissue request
Name in bank records does not match PAN
Ask the bank to correct the name, then validate again
PAN inoperative because it is not linked with Aadhaar

body.title: Open the PDF
body.textWithBlank: The intimation PDF is password protected. The password is your PAN in lower case followed by your date of birth in ___ format.
body.explanation: For example, PAN AFKPS4821M with a date of birth of 14 August 1992 gives afkps4821m14081992. The same convention is used for several documents on the portal.

body.title: The Refund That Never Arrived
body.scenario: Neelam, a physiotherapist in Lucknow, filed and verified her return on 20 July 2026, claiming a refund of ₹19,400. By September nothing has been credited. On the portal her return shows as processed, and the intimation allows the full ₹19,400. Digging further, she finds two things: a refund failure message, because the salary account she nominated was closed when she changed jobs, and an old demand of ₹3,200 for AY 2022-23 that she never knew about.
body.prompt: What is happening, and what should Neelam do, in what order?
body.modelAnswer: Two separate problems are stacking up. First, the refund could not be credited because the nominated account is closed. She should add her current bank account under Profile, then My Bank Account, get it validated, nominate it for refund, and raise a refund reissue request under Services, e-verifying that request. Second, the old demand can reduce what she finally receives. The department can set off a refund against an outstanding demand under Section 245 of the 1961 Act, after giving her an intimation and an opportunity to respond. She should go to Pending Actions, then Response to Outstanding Demand, and check the AY 2022-23 entry. If the demand is genuine, she can agree and pay it, and the balance refund of ₹16,200 comes to her. If it is wrong, for instance because it arose from a TDS credit that was corrected later, she should disagree with reasons, and where it stems from an apparent mistake in an earlier intimation, file a rectification request for that year. What she should not do is wait, because interest keeps running on the demand and the refund stays stuck.

body.title: After You File, Do These Five Things
steps: Watch for the intimation email and open the PDF with your PAN and date of birth
Compare the two columns line by line and find every difference
If a TDS credit was cut, check Form 26AS and follow up with the deductor
If a refund is due but not credited, check that your bank account is validated and nominated, then raise a reissue request
If a demand is raised, respond through Pending Actions rather than ignoring it

points: After e-verification, CPC processes your return and issues an intimation under Section 143(1) of the 1961 Act, which becomes Section 270 of the Income-tax Act, 2025 for later years
The intimation must be issued within nine months from the end of the financial year in which you filed, and refunds are commonly credited about four to five weeks after verification
Read the intimation as two columns and find the line where your figure and the department figure differ
Reduced TDS credit is the most common difference, and it usually means the deductor has not filed or corrected its TDS return
Use a rectification request under Section 154, becoming Section 287, for mistakes apparent from the record, and a revised return for your own errors or omissions
Refunds fail mostly because of bank account problems or an inoperative PAN, and can be set off against old demands under Section 245, re-enacted as Section 438

body.text: This lesson is for educational purposes only and does not constitute tax advice. Processing timelines, portal menus and remedies reflect the position at the time of writing and can change. Responses to demands and notices carry deadlines that depend on the specific communication you receive, so read it carefully and consult a qualified tax professional where the amounts are significant.
